name: Precommitment Devices
description: People will voluntarily adopt costly, binding constraints on their own future choices to counteract anticipated self-control failure (like procrastination), and doing so measurably improves outcomes relative to no constraint -- though self-chosen constraints tend to be less well-calibrated than equivalent externally-imposed ones.
design_relevance_note: Underlies opt-in self-imposed deadlines, spending locks, and 'block this app until you finish X' features -- genuinely user-beneficial when the constraint is transparent and user-initiated, ethically murkier when the product imposes it unasked.
prevalence_note: A recognized, named pattern in behavior-change and productivity-app design specifically, not as universally cross-domain as e.g. loss aversion.

findings.description: Across a field study (MIT executive-education students given the choice to self-impose grade-consequential deadlines for three papers) and follow-up lab studies, people voluntarily self-impose costly, binding deadlines to counteract their own anticipated procrastination, and doing so measurably improves task-completion timing and performance relative to no deadline at all -- but self-set deadlines are not optimally chosen for maximum performance and are less effective than deadlines of equivalent stringency imposed externally (evenly spaced deadlines set by the instructor outperformed self-chosen ones).
findings.source_title: Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment

applications.title: Commitment and reminder nudges reduced stated intent to delay security updates
applications.description: Researchers ran two online experiments (1,000+ participants total) testing whether commitment devices could counter present bias in computer-security behavior. Adding a reminder option reduced stated intent to ignore an automatic-updates prompt by 57% in Study 1; in Study 2, a reminder option reduced willingness to ignore security updates by more than 40% for both Windows and Mac users, and a future-commitment option reduced ignore rates by about 25% for both. The same nudges increased willingness to enroll in two-factor authentication but did not improve uptake of automatic backup tools.
applications.ethical_note: Nudging users toward actions that directly protect their own security (installing patches) with no competing business interest is a clear case of user-beneficial design -- there is no persuasion-for-profit dimension here, only a genuine attempt to close the gap between people's security intentions and their present-biased follow-through.
